findings.location: Section 3.7, 'Base versus instruct (Q2a)' paragraph (sentences citing the GPT-4 report 'highly calibrated' pre-trained model and 'instruction tuning raises ECE by 13.1% on average', then 'The code reason is that an anti-aligned base readout inverts the usual story')
findings.issue: The draft cites only general-NLP evidence that points one way: post-training hurts calibration. That makes Q2a look predictable by analogy, which is the strict reader's A21 clause 2 argument. The L2 interim's load-bearing reason for NARROW was that the NLP direction on post-training is itself contested. Tian et al. reverse the sign for verbal readouts, and the three-stage study finds post-training 'does not uniformly' improve calibration. Neither appears in the draft. Section 3.7 does make the contested-direction argument for reasoning (Q2b), but not for tuning stage.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-l2-residual-post-training-reasoning-format-on-code]], Committed position: 'the supposed general-NLP direction is not established (Tian versus the GPT-4 report on post-training, Yoon versus Barkan and Miao and Ungar on reasoning)'. Tian et al. 2305.14975 [[230514975-just-ask-for-calibration-strategies-for-eliciting-calibrated-confidenc-3]] (abstract-level): 'verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities ... often reducing the expected calibration error by a relative 50%' for RLHF-LMs. [[post-training-shifts-confidence-a-three-stage-analysis-of-how-sft-rl-and-opd-sha]] Table 1: Instruct 0.594, SFT 0.526, RL 0.320, OPD 0.644 Pre-CoT AUROC; text 'post-training does not uniformly improve confidence calibration'. RLCR Table 1: RLVR verbal AUROC 0.50 (HotpotQA) and 0.47 (Big-Math).
findings.recommendation: In the Q2a paragraph, add the countervailing NLP result. Tian et al. find that RLHF verbal confidence is better calibrated than token probabilities, often by a relative 50% in ECE (abstract-level), the opposite of what the GPT-4 report implies for token probabilities. The three-stage math study finds non-monotone AUROC across SFT, RL, and OPD and states that post-training 'does not uniformly' improve calibration. Then say explicitly that the NLP direction on tuning is readout-dependent and contested. That carries the A21 clause 2 argument for Q2a, alongside the DeepSeekCoder anti-aligned base.

findings.location: Section 2.2 (Estimator, Label oracle, and Contamination paragraphs present only fragility evidence); Section 2.5, paragraph beginning 'A strict reader rates each L1 control OCCUPIED'; Section 9.2 'Main risk' sentence
findings.issue: The L1 interim set out a real two-sided dispute. Position B holds that standard practice is adequate, because code studies report concordant rankings across AUROC, ECE, and Brier. The draft gives only Position A and frames the strict reader's objection as 'bundling'. It never cites the concordance evidence, and it never states the interim's committed diagnosis that the dispute is an untested-assumption gap. As a result the predicted null for the protocol (Rank 2's main risk) is under-argued.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-l1-estimator-and-label-oracle-sensitivity-with-contamination-cont]], Position B: 'four-plus code studies report concordant rankings across AUROC, ECE and Brier (2605.28500 App: "broadly consistent")', with the weakness 'nobody tested the claim of adequacy; concordance was reported on closed API models and one benchmark family and without strengthened-test relabeling'. Committed position: 'The disagreement is mostly not factual; it is an untested-assumption gap.' Verified in [[functional-entropy-predicting-functional-correctness-in-llm-generated-code-with]] appendix: 'The calibration results are broadly consistent with the AUROC findings reported in the main text.' Also [[code-is-more-than-text-uncertainty-estimation-for-code-generation]]: 'We do not report Brier Score or ECE: post-hoc rank-normalized scores have no meaningful absolute calibration.'
findings.recommendation: Add a short paragraph to Section 2.2 or 2.5 giving the opposing case. Functional Entropy reports calibration 'broadly consistent with the AUROC findings' across five closed models. Code Is More Than Text declines to report ECE for rank-normalized scores. Standard practice therefore assumes, without testing, that rankings are robust, and that concordance is unverified for open models, under strengthened-test relabeling, and across families. In Section 9.2, name this concordance as the concrete basis for the predicted null, alongside Liu.

findings.issue: The draft supports Q5 with the cross-cell ECE and AUROC decoupling only. The L1 interim holds a sharper result from the same paper that the draft leaves out: a pipeline choice changes ECE substantially while AUROC stays flat. This is the code-side evidence that the measuring instrument, not the readout, can move a ranking, and it bears directly on the 'collapse as validity outcome' design in Section 9.1.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-l1-estimator-and-label-oracle-sensitivity-with-contamination-cont]]: 'Sec 4.4: parse-repair vs fallback-50 moves CodeLlama-7B CoT ECE 0.680 to 0.445 with AUROC 0.556 to 0.546'; 'Sec 4.3: Linguistic has lowest ECE in 4 of 6 models but 3 of those 4 cells are collapsed'; 'CodeLlama-7B Linguistic puts 359/365 at confidence 10'; 'Table 2 (PRR): Direct is best for 4 of 6 models.' Verified in [[verbalized-uncertainty-in-coding-llms-contamination-aware-calibration-uncertainl]]: 'CodeLlama-7B CoT, ECE falls from 0.680 down to 0.445, while AUROC changes from 0.556 to 0.546'.
findings.recommendation: In the Q5 paragraph, add three facts from Tuerlings. Switching the parse policy from parse-repair to a fallback of 50 moves CodeLlama-7B CoT ECE from 0.680 to 0.445 while AUROC barely moves, 0.556 to 0.546 (Section 4.4). Linguistic wins ECE in 4 of 6 models, but 3 of those 4 wins are collapsed cells, and CodeLlama-7B Linguistic puts 359 of 365 at confidence 10 (Sections 4.3 and 4.6). Direct is best on PRR for 4 of 6 models (Table 2). Use these to show that metric choice and parse policy can each reorder verbal formats.

findings.location: Section 3.3, first two paragraphs (Campos within-problem figures) and the paragraph beginning 'The best estimate is therefore that the controlled within-problem gap is small and model-dependent'
findings.issue: The draft gives Campos's within-problem numbers but not the pooled margins of probe over output confidence (Table IV), or the pooled-versus-within pairs for candidate-aware probes (Table V). The probe-confound interim uses both. Without them the reader cannot see that the pooled probe edge on LiveCodeBench and BigCodeBench is already small (+0.029 and +0.006), or how far a candidate-aware probe falls from pooled to within. The draft's estimate also replaces the interim's committed bound (within about 0.05 AUROC, may be zero) with 'small and model-dependent', even though Section 9.5 uses 0.05 as the overturning threshold.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-probe-advantage-real-or-difficulty-confound-on-code]]: Campos 2611.07876 'Table IV (program target, Qwen3-Coder): pooled probe minus confidence is +0.029 on LCB (.844 vs .815), +0.006 on BCB (.656 vs .650), and +0.119 on the in-distribution language sets (.878 vs .759), shrinking to +0.035 under language shift (.790 vs .755)'; 'Table V ... probe on the judging pass has within-problem 0.553 (pooled 0.886); on own generation at last code token 0.620 (pooled 0.895)'. Committed position: 'a probe's within-problem edge over a well-formed own-confidence readout on self-generated code is within about 0.05 AUROC and may be zero' (confidence about 65%).
findings.recommendation: Add the Table IV pooled margins for Qwen3-Coder (+0.029 on LCB, +0.006 on BCB, +0.119 in distribution falling to +0.035 under language shift) and the Table V pairs (judging-pass probe 0.886 pooled against 0.553 within; own-generation last-code-token probe 0.895 pooled against 0.620 within) to Section 3.3 [[which-signals-of-code-correctness-survive-distribution-shift-hidden-state-and-ca]]. Then state the interim's working bound: the within-problem edge is likely within about 0.05 AUROC and may be zero, held at about 65% confidence. That ties the estimate to the 0.05 threshold in Section 9.5.

findings.location: Section 3.2, 'Provenance.' paragraph, and Section 3.3, second paragraph ('The exceptions matter.')
findings.issue: The provenance confound is presented with only the side-B evidence (the follow-up's non-transfer). The probe-confound interim records Position A's best counter, that the code probe survives small semantic mutations, together with a text-surface control in which the probe wins. Both are missing. The disagreement over whether the probe reads style or correctness is therefore blanded out in favor of one side.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-probe-advantage-real-or-difficulty-confound-on-code]], Position A: 'Miglani et al. show the code probe survives small semantic mutations (AUC 0.670 on 392 MBPP+ mutants, 0.692 on 334 HumanEval+ mutants), which argues against pure style'; 'In math, the first-step probe beats a text classifier by 0.20 AUROC (0.79 vs 0.59)' ([[hidden-error-awareness-in-chain-of-thought-reasoningthe-signal-is-diagnostic-not]]). Verified in [[a-heckler-in-the-hidden-statecorrectness-signals-in-diffusion-language-models]]: 'DiffuCoder distinguishes the resulting pass/fail pairs with AUCs of 0.670 on 392 MBPP+ mutants and 0.692 on 334 HumanEval+ mutants. An earlier test on mutations of the model's own code gives an AUC of 0.774. The read therefore survives when passing and failing programs differ by small edits rather than broad changes in style.'
findings.recommendation: After the follow-up's 37.1-point non-transfer result, add the counter-evidence. A DiffuCoder probe still separates pass and fail mutants that differ by small edits: AUC 0.670 on 392 MBPP+ mutants, 0.692 on 334 HumanEval+ mutants, and 0.774 on mutations of the model's own code [[a-heckler-in-the-hidden-statecorrectness-signals-in-diffusion-language-models]]. Outside code, a first-step probe beats a TF-IDF text-surface classifier by 0.79 to 0.59 [[hidden-error-awareness-in-chain-of-thought-reasoningthe-signal-is-diagnostic-not]]. Conclude, as the interim does, that provenance is a plausible but unproven explanation of Ribeiro's margin, and that the sign-reversed likelihood baseline in Section 9.1 item 4 is the test that decides it.

findings.location: Section 9.1, 'Evidence the paper must generate', item 1 ('at least 100 mixed-outcome problems per model') and item 6 ('base-versus-instruct and same-weights reasoning arms'); Section 9.5 first bullet (0.05 margin)
findings.issue: The design specification drops the concrete prescriptions in the L2 interim. These cover how many base and instruct pairs to use, the base-model elicitation guard, how to toggle reasoning and where to read the probe, and the sample-size floor needed to resolve effects near the 0.05 margin the report itself uses as its decision threshold. With 100 mixed problems the design may be underpowered for that threshold, and the draft does not say so.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-l2-residual-post-training-reasoning-format-on-code]], Committed position, prescriptive consequences: '(2) base models need a base-compatible readout (P(True)-style yes/no token probability or few-shot numeric with a >=3-distinct-values guard, per Ghosh's H3 failure)'; '(3) the reasoning toggle must be the same weights (for example Qwen3 thinking on/off) ... with the probe read at a fixed position (prompt-final and answer-boundary) and a prompt-length residualization control (2606.14530: 0.881 to 0.842 versus a 0.657 baseline)'; '(5) at least three base/instruct pairs from different families, with AUROC differences judged by problem-clustered paired bootstrap (Rathnasuriya's own CI on dAUC is [-0.0911, 0.0652] for OpenCoder, so n of about 400+ problems per cell is the realistic floor to resolve effects near 0.05)'.
findings.recommendation: In item 6, specify the extension: at least three base and instruct pairs from different families; a base-compatible readout (P(True)-style or few-shot numeric) with a guard requiring at least three distinct values; and a same-weights reasoning toggle (for example Qwen3 thinking on and off), with the probe read at prompt-final and answer-boundary positions and a prompt-length residualization control. In item 1, note that resolving differences near the 0.05 threshold of Section 9.5 likely needs about 400 or more problems per cell, per the interim's reading of the OpenCoder interval, and treat 100 mixed problems as a minimum rather than a target.

findings.location: Section 2.2, 'Label oracle (Q10)' paragraph (ends 'Q10 is CLEAN (provisional).'); Section 8 row 'L1 | Q10 test insufficiency changes rankings | Prov. | Nearest: EvalPlus (accuracy); SWE-ABS (agents); Liu (SQL)'

Selective generation [[towards-functional-correctness-of-code-models-with-selective-generation]] (Section 5.2.2) shows on code that its false-discovery-rate guarantee tightens as more fuzz-generated tests label the outputs. findings.location: Section 3.2, 'Supervision asymmetry.' paragraph, last sentence ('The only partial code control is Gros and Devanbu's Platt scaling of every readout; ... their Qwen line-level gap (probe 0.83 against line-verbalized 0.71) survives it')

It also gives the Platt-scaled BSS for both models. These figures sharpen the claim that the size of the code probe margin depends on who supplies the hidden states.
findings.evidence: Interim [[interim-report-probe-advantage-real-or-difficulty-confound-on-code]]: Gros and Devanbu Tables 3-4: 'GPT-4o: Line Verbalized AUC 0.75, scaled BSS 0.17; Probe-7B AUC 0.78, scaled BSS 0.22 ... Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct: Line Verbalized AUC 0.71, scaled BSS 0.10; Probe-7B AUC 0.83, scaled BSS 0.33'; 'the probe margin over GPT-4o's own verbalized readout (+0.03 AUC, +0.05 BSS) is a supervised external reader's margin.'
findings.recommendation: Extend the sentence with the GPT-4o result. The margin is 0.78 against 0.75 AUC and 0.22 against 0.17 Platt-scaled BSS, where the 'probe' is a separate 0.5B or 7B reader. For Qwen, where the probe reads the generator's own states, it is 0.83 against 0.71 AUC and 0.33 against 0.10 scaled BSS [[localized-calibrated-uncertainty-in-code-language-models]].
